title: Is nothing born of matter immortal?
source_text: Φησὶ δ᾿ ὅτι καὶ ὕλης ἔκγονον οὐδὲν ἀθάνατον. καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο λελέξεται ὅτι, εἴπερ ὕλης οὐδὲν ἔκγονον ἀθάνατον, ἤτοι ἀθάνατος ὅλος ὁ κόσμος καὶ οὐχ ὡς ὕλης ἐστὶν ἔκγονον ἢ οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς χρῆμά ἐστιν ἀθάνατον. εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀθάνατος ὁ κόσμος, ὅπερ ἀρέσκει καὶ τοῖς θεοῦ ἔργον εἰποῦσι μόνην τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ ἀπό τινος αὐτὴν κρατῆρος γεγονέναι λέγουσι. δεικνύτω ὁ Κέλσος οὐκ ἐξ ὕλης ἀποίου αὐτὸν γεγονέναι, τηρῶν τὸ ὕλης ἔκγονον οὐδὲν ἀθάνατον· εἰ δ᾿, ἐπεὶ ὕλης ἔκγονόν ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος, οὐκ ἔστιν ἀθάνατον ὁ κόσμος· θνητὸν ὁ κόσμος ἆρ᾿ οὖν καὶ φθειρόμενον ἢ μή; εἰ μὲν γὰρ φθειρόμενον, ὡς θεοῦ ἔργον ἔσται φθειρόμενον· εἶτ᾿ ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ ἔργον τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ ψυχὴ τί ποιήσει. λεγέτω ὁ Κέλσος· εἰ δὲ διαστρέφων τὴν ἔννοιαν τοῦ ἀθανάτου φήσει τῷ φθαρτῷ μὲν οὐ φθειρομένῳ δὲ ἀθάνατον αὐτὸν εἶναι, ὡς δεκτικὸν μὲν θανάτου οὐ μὴν δὲ καὶ ἀποθνῄσκοντα. δῆλον ὅτι ἔσται τι κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον θνητὸν ἅμα καὶ ἀθάνατον τῷ ἀμφοτέρων εἶναι δεκτικὸν, καὶ ἔσται θνητὸν οὐκ ἀποθνῇσκον, καὶ τὸ οὐ τῇ φύσει ἀθάνατον παρὰ τὸ μὴ ἀποθνῄσκειν ἰδίως λεγόμενον ἀθάνατον. κατὰ ποῖον οὖν σημαινόμενον διαστελλόμενος φήσει ὕλης ἔκγονον οὐδὲν ἀθάνατον; καὶ ὁρᾷς ὅτι πιεζόμενα αὐτὰ καὶ βασανιζόμενα τὰ ἐν τοῖς γράμμασι νοήματα διελέγχεται οὐκ ἐπιδεχόμενα τὸ γενναῖον καὶ ἀναντίῤῥητον. εἰπὼν δὲ ταῦτ᾿ ἐπιφέρει ὅτι τοῦδε μὲν πέρι ἀπόχρη τοσαῦτα· καὶ εἴ τις ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀκούειν δύναιτο καὶ ζητεῖν. εἴσεται. ἴδωμεν οὖν ἡμεῖς οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀνόητοι, τί ἠκολούθησε τῷ κἂν ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον ἡμᾶς αὐτοῦ ἀκούειν δυνηθῆναι καὶ ζητεῖν.
pass_a_gloss: And he says (φησί) that 'of matter (ὕλης) nothing [is] an offspring (ἔκγονον) immortal (ἀθάνατον)'. And to this it will be said that, if nothing offspring of matter [is] immortal, either the whole world (κόσμος) is immortal and is not as offspring of matter, or neither is it itself an immortal thing (χρῆμα). If then the world [is] immortal -- which pleases (ἀρέσκει) also those who said only the soul (ψυχήν) [is] the work (ἔργον) of God and say it came to be from some mixing bowl (κρατῆρος) -- let Celsus show (δεικνύτω) it to have come to be not from qualityless (ἀποίου) matter, keeping (τηρῶν) 'nothing offspring of matter immortal'. But if, since the world is offspring of matter, the world is not immortal, [is] the world mortal (θνητόν) then and perishing (φθειρόμενον) or not? For if perishing, as a work of God it will be perishing; then in the destruction (φθορᾷ) of the world what will the work of God, the soul, do? Let Celsus say (λεγέτω). But if, perverting (διαστρέφων) the notion (ἔννοιαν) of the immortal, he will say it is immortal by the perishable (φθαρτῷ) but not perishing, as receptive (δεκτικόν) of death (θανάτου) yet not dying (ἀποθνῄσκοντα), it is clear that there will be according to him something mortal and at once immortal by being receptive of both, and it will be mortal not dying, and what is not by nature (φύσει) immortal [is] properly/specially (ἰδίως) called immortal by not dying. According to what kind of meaning (σημαινόμενον) then, distinguishing (διαστελλόμενος), will he say 'nothing offspring of matter immortal'? And you see that, pressed (πιεζόμενα) and tested by torture (βασανιζόμενα), the thoughts (νοήματα) in the writings (γράμμασι) are refuted (διελέγχεται), not admitting (ἐπιδεχόμενα) the noble/sound (γενναῖον) and incontestable (ἀναντίρρητον). And having said these things he adds (ἐπιφέρει): 'about this so much suffices (ἀπόχρη); and if anyone could hear (ἀκούειν) further and inquire (ζητεῖν), he will know (εἴσεται)'. Let us then see, we the senseless (ἀνόητοι) according to him, what followed (ἠκολούθησε) on our being able even a little to hear him and inquire.
pass_b_english: He says also that “nothing born of matter is immortal.” To this it will be said that, if nothing born of matter is immortal, then either the whole world is immortal and is not something born of matter, or the world itself is not an immortal thing either.

If, then, the world is immortal, which is the view even of those who said that only the soul is God’s work and who say that it came from a mixing bowl (Plato, Timaeus 41d), let Celsus show that the world did not come into being from matter without qualities, if he is to keep his saying that “nothing born of matter is immortal.” But if, since the world is born of matter, the world is not immortal, is the world then mortal, and does it perish, or not? For if it perishes, it will perish as a work of God. Then, when the world perishes, what will the soul, the work of God, do? Let Celsus tell us.

But suppose he twists the notion of “immortal” and says that the world is immortal by being perishable and yet not perishing, as being capable of death but not in fact dying. Then plainly, on his view, there will be something at once mortal and immortal, by being capable of both; there will be a mortal thing that does not die; and what is not immortal by nature will be called immortal in a special sense, because it does not die. In what sense of the word, then, will he be drawing his distinction when he says that “nothing born of matter is immortal”? And you see that the ideas in his writings, when they are pressed and put to the test, are shown up as admitting nothing sound and beyond dispute.

After saying this he adds: “On this subject so much is enough; and if anyone is able to hear and inquire further, he will know.” Let us then, who are without understanding in his view, see what has come of our being able to hear him and inquire even a little.

choices.choice: κατὰ ποῖον σημαινόμενον διαστελλόμενος: 'In what meaning ... will he draw his distinction' -> 'In what sense of the word ... will he be drawing his distinction'
translator note: added that Celsus shares the soul-only view (4.52-54)
Timaeus 41d (mixing bowl, κρατήρ) checked; Celsus's quoted words and Origen's reply kept distinct

Those 'who said that only the soul is God's work and that it came from a mixing bowl' are Plato and his followers (and Celsus with them, who in 4.52-54 made the soul alone God's work): the mixing bowl is Timaeus 41d, already named in 4.56; Plato's view that the generated world will not be dissolved (Timaeus 41a-b) lies behind 'perishable yet not perishing', but only the certain reference (41d) is cited inline. 'If it perishes, it will perish as a work of God' (ὡς θεοῦ ἔργον ἔσται φθειρόμενον): Koetschau punctuates as a statement, not a question; the point is that a work of God would then perish, against Celsus's claim that God makes nothing mortal. 'Without understanding' (ἀνόητοι) answers Celsus's charge that Christians are senseless. No Scripture quoted.
